text: CHAPTER TWO: FRAMING ANALYTICS PROBLEMS
Prepared by: Inst. Caesar Gabriel M. Fernando
Learning Outcomes
At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:
Analyze organizational context and stakeholder needs.
Differentiate situation, symptom, issue, problem, opportunity, question, and decision.
Formulate decision-oriented analytics questions.
Define objectives, requirements, metrics, KPIs, success criteria, scope, constraints, assumptions, risks, and expected value.
Develop a coherent analytics project charter that aligns problem, evidence, outputs, and organizational value.
OPENING CASE: Fulfillment & Service Analytics

NEXUS Fulfillment Services manages order preparation, packing, dispatch, and last-mile coordination for several online merchants. During the past three months, management has reported that the company is processing more orders than ever before and that average warehouse productivity has improved. Despite these apparent gains, customer complaints about delayed deliveries have increased, more orders are missing their promised delivery dates, and several merchant partners have begun questioning whether NEXUS can maintain its service-level commitments during periods of high demand. Operations managers believe the problem is insufficient delivery capacity, while warehouse supervisors argue that orders are already being packed on time and that delays occur after dispatch. Customer-service teams claim that many complaints involve poor status updates rather than actual late deliveries, while management suspects that certain merchants, locations, order types, or delivery partners may be responsible for a disproportionate share of the service failures. NEXUS has access to order timestamps, promised delivery dates, picking and packing times, dispatch records, courier assignments, delivery completion times, order priority, merchant information, destination zones, customer complaints, and service-status updates. Management now needs to determine whether the organization is facing a warehouse fulfillment problem, a delivery-capacity problem, a service-communication problem, a customer-expectation problem, or some combination of these, before deciding where additional resources or process changes should be directed.
OPENING CASE: What exactly is the problem?
notes: Do not analyze the data yet.
Do not choose a model yet.
Do not recommend a dashboard yet.
First ask:
What is merely a symptom?
What could be the underlying problem?
Who are the relevant stakeholders?
What decisions does management actually need to make?
What information would be required to distinguish among the competing explanations?
What would “better fulfillment performance” actually mean?

text: Analytics work need structure
Based on the NEXUS case, we could:
examine warehouse processing times;
compare courier performance;
investigate destination zones;
analyze customer complaints;
forecast delivery demand;
classify orders likely to become late;
optimize courier assignment;
redesign status notifications.
All of these may be legitimate analytics activities.
But this creates another problem:
In what order should we do them—and how do we know which ones are actually necessary?

text: Before the Algorithm Comes the Process
Many often think of analytics as:
Data → Algorithm → Result
A more realistic view is:
Problem → Stakeholders → Decision → Questions → Evidence → Data → Preparation → Analysis/Model → Evaluation → Communication → Action → Deployment → Monitoring
The algorithm may occupy only one part of this chain.
This is precisely why professional analytics has developed frameworks, process models, methodologies, and life-cycle models.

text: Analytics work need structure

Analytics work consists not only of performing calculations or constructing models, but of coordinating a sequence of activities that connects an organizational need with relevant data, analytical methods, interpretation, decisions, implementation, and evaluation.
Without structure, technically competent analysts can still:
solve the wrong problem;
use irrelevant data;
optimize the wrong metric;
build an unnecessary model;
produce results too late to support the decision;
or develop a solution that nobody actually uses.

text: What Is an Analytics Framework?

A structured, end-to-end conceptual and architectural methodology that systematically governs the acquisition, transformation, modeling, and interpretation of data to support decision-making, optimize organizational performance, and generate actionable insights. (Delen & Demirkan, 2013; INFORMS, 2020)
For this course, an analytics framework may be understood as an organized structure that guides how an analytics initiative is conceptualized, performed, evaluated, and connected to its intended use.
A framework may help answer questions such as:
Where should an analytics project begin?
How should the problem be understood?
When should data be examined?
When should modeling occur?
How should results be evaluated?
Who needs to be involved?
How does a result become an operational solution?
What happens after deployment?
notes: Important Qualification
Not every framework we will examine is the same kind of framework.
Some were created primarily for knowledge discovery.
Some for data mining projects.
Some for model development.
Some for team-based data science and production systems.
And some attempt to structure the entire organizational analytics lifecycle.
That difference is important.

text: Framework, Methodology, Process Model, and Lifecycle
These terms are often used loosely, but they are not necessarily identical.
Term
Definition
Framework

A high-level conceptual and architectural structure that defines the taxonomy (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive), technological capabilities, and strategic pillars needed to organize analytics within an enterprise.
Methodology
A codified system of principles, analytical techniques, statistical practices, and validation rules systematically applied to formulate, solve, and evaluate data problems.
Process Model
A formalized, step-by-step workflow representation depicting the sequential phases, task dependencies, iterative loops, and deliverables of an analytical project.
Lifecycle

The complete operational timeline through which an analytical model or data product evolves—from business problem framing and data acquisition to model deployment, monitoring, drift management, retraining, and retirement.
notes: Important
A framework tells us how to think about the work.
A methodology may tell us how to perform portions of the work.
A lifecycle reminds us that analytics may continue after the model has been created.
Important

text: Why Are There Different Analytics Frameworks?
Because analytics itself evolved from several traditions.
Modern analytics brings together ideas from:
Statistics + Operations Research + Databases + Knowledge Discovery + Data Mining + Machine Learning + Information Systems + Decision Science + Software Engineering + Business Analysis
Different frameworks therefore emphasize different parts of the journey.
Example
A researcher interested in discovering patterns from a very large database has different needs from:
a data scientist deploying a predictive API;
a consultant framing an executive decision;
an operations team redesigning fulfillment;
or an organization maintaining hundreds of analytical solutions.
notes: There should therefore be no expectation that one historical framework was designed to solve every modern analytics problem.

text: KDD: Knowledge Discovery Is More Than Data Mining
Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) refers to the broader, iterative process through which useful and understandable patterns or knowledge are identified from data.
A key contribution of the KDD literature is the distinction between KDD and data mining:
KDD = the complete knowledge-discovery process.
Data Mining = the computational step in which algorithms are applied to extract patterns from data.
notes: Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro, and Smyth characterize KDD as the nontrivial process of identifying patterns that are valid, novel, potentially useful, and understandable.
Central lesson:
An algorithm may discover a pattern.
Human interpretation determines whether that pattern becomes knowledge.

text: CRISP-DM: From Business Understanding to Deployment
CRISP-DM stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining.
It is a widely used process model that organizes a data-mining project around six interrelated phases:
Business Understanding → Data Understanding → Data Preparation → Modeling → Evaluation → Deployment
Unlike a purely technical workflow, CRISP-DM explicitly begins with the business problem rather than the algorithm.
notes: Central idea
Analytical modeling should be driven by organizational objectives—not merely by available data or preferred techniques.

So CRISP-DM gets us much closer—but we still need a broader umbrella.

text: SEMMA: A Modeling-Centered Analytics Process
SEMMA represents:
Sample → Explore → Modify → Model → Assess
Developed in association with SAS, SEMMA organizes the core technical activities involved in developing and assessing data-mining models.
Its primary center of gravity is different from CRISP-DM.
CRISP-DM begins with Business Understanding.
SEMMA begins much closer to the analytical dataset.
notes: Central idea
Once the analytical problem and data are available, how should we systematically explore, prepare, model, and evaluate them?

text: From Question to Sustained Organizational Value

The INFORMS Analytics Framework (IAF) is a comprehensive structure designed to guide analytics practitioners through the entire lifecycle of an analytics initiative—from the initial business concept to sustained, value-delivering operations.
INFORMS describes its central philosophy succinctly:
Analytics does not begin with data. It begins with a question.
It also emphasizes that analytics does not end when a model has been developed.
It treats analytics as a connected life cycle rather than a model-building exercise.
The IAF places the business or mission question before data, methods, and models.
Problem framing asks what decision, need, opportunity, or uncertainty deserves analytical support before the team chooses data or technology.
notes: Central idea
A useful model may eventually have to become a reproducible, deployable and maintainable analytical product.

text: INFORMS Does Not Replace the Other Frameworks

Frameworks can complement one another. Selecting the INFORMS Analytics Framework as the course's umbrella framework does not mean that KDD, CRISP-DM, SEMMA, TDSP, or other methodologies become obsolete. They address different scopes and may provide useful practices within different parts of an analytics initiative.

Other Frameworks That May Inform the Work (Suggested Only, Not Official)

I–II: Problem Framing
CRISP-DM Business Understanding
Helps connect organizational objectives to analytics work.
III: Data

Selection, understanding, preprocessing, transformation, data quality.
IV–V: Method Selection & Development
KDD, CRISP-DM, SEMMA
Exploration, preparation, modeling, pattern discovery, assessment and validation.
V–VI: Development & Deployment
CRISP-DM, TDSP
Reproducible model development and movement toward implementation.
VI–VII: Deployment & Life Cycle
TDSP, MLOps practices
Productionization, monitoring, updating, versioning and maintenance.

text: The Seven Domains of the INFORMS Analytics Framework
Domain
Source-grounded purpose
Guiding question
I. Business Problem (Question) Framing
Establish a clear organizational problem, question, or opportunity; identify stakeholders, sponsors, beneficiaries, scope, expected benefits, costs, and organizational effects.
What problem actually matters, to whom, and why?
II. Analytics Problem Framing

Translate the agreed business problem into an actionable analytical structure; identify the analytics type, conceptual drivers/inputs, outputs, assumptions, success measures, baseline, and initial risks.
What must analytics determine?
III. Data
Identify the data needed and available and prepare, document, and manage it so that it can support the analytical problem.
What evidence do we need, and can we trust it for this use?
IV. Methodology (Approach) Selection
Determine the analytical approaches and techniques appropriate for the framed problem and available evidence.
How should the problem be analyzed?
V. Analytics / Model Development
Develop, test, validate, interpret, and evaluate the analytical solution.
Does the analytical approach work adequately?
VI. Deployment
Put the analytics solution into operational use and connect it to users, processes, and decisions.
How will the solution actually be used?
VII. Analytics Solution Life Cycle Management
Sustain the analytical solution by monitoring its effectiveness, relevance, performance, risk, and continuing value.
Does it remain useful after deployment?
Why the INFORMS Analytics Framework Is Not Waterfall
A logical progression does not mean a rigid sequence.
The seven IAF domains are usually presented as:
I. Business Problem Framing → II. Analytics Problem Framing → III. Data → IV. Methodology Selection → V. Analytics/Model Development → VI. Deployment → VII. Life Cycle Management

However, INFORMS explicitly describes these domains as “connected and iterative, not sequential.” Work completed in a later domain may reveal problems that require the team to return to and revise an earlier domain.

text: Why the INFORMS Analytics Framework Is Not Waterfall
Why IAF is not Waterfall
Example
Later findings can change earlier framing.
During Data, NEXUS discovers that courier pickup timestamps are unreliable → return to Analytics Problem Framing and revise what can actually be investigated.
Methods may need to be reconsidered.
During Model Development, predictive performance is too weak → return to Data or Methodology Selection.
Deployment can expose usability problems.
An SLA-risk model works technically, but operations staff cannot act on predictions quickly enough → revisit the problem, output, or model design.
The environment changes after deployment.
New courier partners or changing demand patterns reduce model reliability → Life Cycle Management triggers recalibration or reframing.
Stakeholder feedback continues throughout the lifecycle.
Management changes its priority from reducing lateness to improving merchant retention → earlier objectives and analytics questions may need revision.
notes: Waterfall vs. IAF
Waterfall:Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3 → Phase 4Complete one stage, then proceed primarily forward.
INFORMS IAF:I ⇄ II ⇄ III ⇄ IV ⇄ V ⇄ VI ⇄ VIIProgress through the lifecycle, but revisit earlier domains whenever evidence, stakeholder needs, or operating conditions require it.

text: Domain I — Business Problem (Question) Framing
Business Problem Framing defines the organizational or mission-level challenge before it becomes a technical problem.
The frame may begin from a problem to solve, a question to answer, or an opportunity to explore.
Its purpose is to establish what matters, to whom it matters, what is within scope, and whether analytics is an appropriate way to help.
A strong Domain I frame ends with stakeholder agreement on the problem and direction—not with a chosen algorithm.
Domain I asks whether the team understands the organizational problem, opportunity, stakeholders, scope, expected benefits, and consequences.
Domain I — What Must Be Established
A clear problem/question/opportunity statement.
Relevant stakeholders, sponsors, decision-makers, users, and beneficiaries.
Scope and what the project can realistically influence.
Expected benefits, costs, risks, consequences, and organizational effects.
Whether the problem is genuinely amenable to analytics.
Explicit agreement on the problem before significant technical work begins.

Domain I element
What we must be able to say

text: Domain I — Guiding Questions
Are we dealing with a problem, a question, an opportunity, or some combination?
What is still unclear or undefined?
What is inside and outside the team’s ability to influence?
Who has a vested stake, and whose perspective is missing?
What benefits, costs, risks, and indirect consequences could follow from a solution?
Is analytics actually appropriate, or is the real issue a broken process, missing policy, unavailable data, or lack of authority?
What must stakeholders agree on before the project proceeds?
Domain II — Analytics Problem Framing
Analytics Problem Framing translates the agreed organizational problem into an actionable analytical structure.

This translation still occurs at the business/conceptual level: the team defines decisions, objectives, relationships, inputs, outputs, measures, assumptions, constraints, and risks before coding or modeling.
The task is not merely to rename the business problem as “machine learning.” It is to determine what kind of evidence and analytical reasoning can support the decision.
Domain II closes with stakeholder agreement on the analytics approach.
notes: Lecture expansion / speaker note: This domain is the direct academic home of many Week 2 topics in the course plan: analytics questions, objectives, KPIs, success criteria, scope, assumptions, constraints, risks, and expected value.

text: Domain I vs. Domain II — Do Not Collapse Them
Domain I asks whether we are solving the right organizational challenge.
Domain II asks whether we have translated that challenge into the right analytical structure.
The distinction protects the class from tool-driven framing and from mistaking a business outcome for a modeling target.
Both domains require stakeholder communication and agreement.

text: Communication Checkpoints — Agreement Is Part of Analytics
The IAF treats stakeholder alignment as a formal part of the analytics process, not as presentation work added at the end.
A communication checkpoint asks whether stakeholders and analysts share the same understanding of the problem, scope, success, and analytical direction.
Agreement does not mean everyone has identical interests. It means disagreements, trade-offs, responsibilities, and boundaries are visible enough to proceed responsibly.
When later evidence contradicts assumptions, the team may need to return to an earlier checkpoint.
notes: Note: This helps students see communication as analytical infrastructure. Misalignment can invalidate an otherwise technically sound project because the solution no longer addresses what decision-makers or beneficiaries actually need.

text: What Is an Ambiguous Organizational Situation?
An ambiguous situation is a real-world condition in which something appears important, undesirable, uncertain, or promising, but the underlying need and appropriate action are not yet clear.
Ambiguity may come from incomplete evidence, conflicting stakeholder interpretations, multiple plausible causes, unclear objectives, or competing constraints.
Analytics begins by structuring this ambiguity—not by pretending it has already disappeared.

text: Example of Ambiguity: NOVA Retail
Management observes that July orders are higher than June, yet profitability appears weaker.

Possible interpretations include: higher discount intensity; channel mix change; lower-margin product mix; acquisition-heavy customer mix; rising cost; returns; incomplete data; or a combination of these.
The observation is important, but it is not yet a proven explanation.
notes: This case is ideal because it forces students to separate what is directly observed from what still has to be investigated.

text: Why Ambiguity Is Not a Failure
Ambiguity is normal at the beginning of analysis because organizations operate as interconnected systems.
A single observed outcome may have several contributing factors.
Stakeholders can also describe the same condition differently because their objectives differ.
Professional analysis makes uncertainty explicit and progressively reduces it.
notes: This case is ideal because it forces students to separate what is directly observed from what still has to be investigated.

An anomaly is an observation or pattern that differs substantially from what is expected, typical, or historically observed.
Anomaly does not mean error: it may represent a valid but unusual event.
Before interpreting an anomaly, check data quality, context, seasonality, and relevant comparison groups

text: Symptom
A symptom is an observable sign that a condition may require attention.
Symptoms describe manifestations of a problem, not necessarily its underlying cause.
Examples: falling profit, rising complaint volume, low attendance, high churn, long waiting time, declining donations.
A symptom identifies where attention may be needed; it does not establish the underlying cause.

text: Problem
IIBA defines a business problem as an issue of strategic or tactical importance that prevents an enterprise or organization from achieving its goals.
Working analytics definition: an underlying condition, need, risk, or obstacle that requires understanding or action because it affects desired outcomes.
A problem statement should be decision-relevant rather than merely descriptive.
Example:
Current state: 86% SLA compliance.
Desired state: ≥95% SLA compliance.
Gap:
9 percentage points.
But the underlying problem still needs formulation.
notes: In social or advocacy contexts, “problem” should not imply that people themselves are the problem. Frame the condition, system, process, access gap, or resource mismatch.

text: Need
IIBA defines a need as a problem or opportunity to be addressed.
Need is broader than problem: it can arise because something is failing, but also because improvement or innovation is possible.
Analytics should therefore support both corrective and opportunity-seeking work.
Example:
An NGO needs a more equitable way to allocate limited assistance.
A need is a required condition, capability, resource, or improvement necessary to achieve an objective or serve stakeholders.

text: Opportunity
An opportunity is a favorable condition or possibility that may create value if recognized and acted upon.
Opportunity analytics may ask where growth, improvement, efficiency, reach, or service quality could be increased.
Example: a channel with high repeat-purchase behavior may be an opportunity even if no current “problem” exists.
Even if SLA performance were acceptable, analytics might identify an opportunity to:
reduce fulfillment time;
improve courier allocation;
improve proactive communication;
offer differentiated service levels.

text: Issue
An issue is a current condition already requiring attention because it is affecting objectives, operations, stakeholders, or performance.
An issue differs from a risk because the issue exists now, while risk concerns uncertainty about future effects on objectives.
Example: missing customer IDs in the current dataset are an issue; the possibility that future system changes will break ID consistency is a risk.

text: Root Cause
A root cause is a deeper condition that generates or sustains a problem.
Root-cause language should be used carefully: identifying a plausible explanation is not the same as establishing causal evidence.
In analytics, the phrase “possible contributing factor” is often more defensible until stronger evidence is available.

text: Problem Framing
Problem framing is the disciplined process of defining the need, context, stakeholders, objectives, boundaries, and decision before selecting analytical methods.
A frame determines what is treated as relevant, what is excluded, and what success means.
Because different frames lead to different analytics projects, framing is an analytical decision in its own right.
notes: CRISP-DM Business Understanding and IIBA Business Analysis converge on this idea: understand the organizational need and value before technical execution.

text: Why Framing Changes the Analytics
Frame A: “How can we increase sales?” may prioritize revenue, promotion, and acquisition.
Frame B: “How can we grow profitably?” prioritizes margin, costs, discounts, and customer/product mix.
Frame C: “How can we improve customer lifetime value?” prioritizes retention, repeat behavior, cohort value, and experience.
Same organization, different frame, different data and methods.
notes: CRISP-DM Business Understanding and IIBA Business Analysis converge on this idea: understand the organizational need and value before technical execution.
Framing does not merely describe a problem—it establishes the boundaries through which the problem will be understood.

text: Problem Statement
A problem statement is a concise, evidence-aware description of the condition requiring understanding or action, why it matters, and the decision it should support.
It should identify the stakeholder or context, the observed gap or need, and the intended decision without assuming an unproven cause.
A problem statement is not a solution statement.
Problem Framing
What situation are we dealing with?
Problem Formulation
How precisely should we represent the problem so it can be investigated and acted upon?
notes: Avoid embedding the answer inside the problem: “The problem is excessive discounts” is too early if excessive discounts have not yet been established as the main driver.

text: Weak vs. Strong Problem Statements
Weak statements are tool-driven, vague, causal without evidence, or disconnected from a decision.
Weak statement
What is wrong with it
Stronger reframing
Analyze our sales data
No problem or decision
Management needs to understand why July growth did not translate into stronger gross profit so it can adjust pricing, channel, or category strategy.
Build a churn model
Method before need
Customer success needs to identify customers at elevated risk of disengagement early enough to prioritize retention action.
Discounts caused lower profit
Unproven causal claim
Management needs to determine whether discount intensity, channel mix, product mix, or customer mix are associated with weaker profitability.
notes: The strong version names the stakeholder, observed condition, consequence, uncertainty, and decision need.

text: Problem Statement Formula
Practical template: “[Stakeholder] needs to understand/address [condition or need] because [consequence/value], so that [decision or action] can be improved.”
Optional extension: include the relevant time horizon, population, or process.
Do not name a model or tool unless it is genuinely part of a non-negotiable solution requirement.
notes: This formula is a teaching scaffold, not a universal standard. It helps students produce a decision-oriented statement before they learn more sophisticated requirements documentation.

text: Decision
A decision is a choice among possible courses of action.
Decisions are made in relation to objectives and constraints, and often under uncertainty.
Analytics is valuable when it changes the information available for that choice or helps evaluate alternatives.
notes: Note: Distinguish a decision from a prediction. “Who will churn?” is a prediction question; “Whom should we contact, when, and with what intervention?” is a decision question.

text: Decision-Maker
A decision-maker is the person or group with responsibility or authority to choose, approve, or authorize an action.
The decision-maker may not be the same as the data owner, end user, analyst, or beneficiary.
Analytics communication should be shaped around the decision-maker’s information needs and authority.
Example:
Head of Fulfillment Operations who must decide whether to add delivery capacity, change courier allocation, revise cutoff times, or redesign fulfillment procedures.
notes: Note: Identifying a decision-maker prevents recommendations such as “the company should…” when no actual role has been identified as capable of acting.

text: Decision Context
Decision context includes the objective, available alternatives, timing, constraints, uncertainty, costs, consequences, and stakeholder implications surrounding a choice.
The same analytical result can lead to different actions under different decision contexts.
Example: a 20% churn probability may trigger action if intervention is cheap, but not if intervention is costly or intrusive.
notes: Note: This prepares students for thresholds, cost-sensitive evaluation, optimization, and prescriptive analytics later in the course.

Baselines may be historical performance, current practice, a simple model, a control group, or a “do nothing” scenario.
Without a baseline, improvement claims can become meaningless.

text: Decision-Driven Analytics
Decision-Driven Analytics
Decision-driven analytics begins by identifying the decision that needs to improve, then determines what evidence, data, analysis, and tools are needed.
It contrasts with tool-driven analytics, which begins from a preferred technology and searches for a use case.
Decision-driven does not mean ignoring methods; it means method selection is justified by decision needs.
notes: Note: This is one of the core philosophical distinctions of the course.

text: Problem-Driven vs. Decision-Driven Analytics
Problem-driven analytics begins from a real-world need or problem.
Decision-driven analytics begins from a choice or action that needs better evidence.
They are complementary: a problem explains why the project exists; the decision identifies how analytics can create value.
notes: Note: A good project can be expressed both ways: “What problem matters?” and “What decision can change because of the evidence?”

text: Tool-Driven Analytics
Tool-driven analytics begins with a preferred technology, model, platform, or algorithm and then searches for a problem that justifies its use.
This can create “solutionism”: choosing a solution before confirming the need.
Examples: “We need AI,” “Let us use deep learning,” “We should make a dashboard,” “We should build a chatbot.”
notes: Note: Tool experimentation is useful for learning, but an organizational recommendation should explain why the tool is appropriate, feasible, and valuable for the need.

text: Method-Driven Analytics
Method-driven analytics starts from a desired analytical technique such as clustering, classification, forecasting, or optimization.
It may produce technically interesting outputs that fail to answer the organization’s actual question.
A method becomes justified only after the question, target, evidence requirements, and decision context are clear.
notes: Note: This is particularly important because students already know many analytics techniques from prerequisite courses.

text: Domain Subject-Matter Expert
IIBA describes a domain subject-matter expert as a stakeholder with in-depth knowledge relevant to the business need or solution scope.
Domain experts help interpret what variables mean, which patterns are plausible, and which recommendations are operationally realistic.
Domain knowledge is evidence context, not a substitute for data validation.
Example:
Warehouse supervisor who understands picking, packing, staging, dispatch handoffs, cutoff times, and operational bottlenecks that may not be obvious from the data alone.

text: Context
IIBA defines context as the circumstances that influence, are influenced by, and provide understanding of a change.
In analytics, context determines how observations should be interpreted and what factors may matter.
Context can include time, place, process, policy, culture, market conditions, weather, institutional rules, available resources, and stakeholder behavior.
Organizational Context
Organizational context includes goals, structure, roles, processes, policies, culture, resources, technology, and performance expectations.
A metric has meaning only relative to organizational purpose.
Example: “delivery time = 48 hours” may be acceptable in one service model and a failure in another.
External Context
External context includes environmental factors outside direct organizational control that influence interpretation or decisions.
Examples: regulation, economy, seasonality, competitors, weather, public policy, demographics, events, supply conditions, or social trends.
External context can explain apparent anomalies that internal data alone cannot.
notes: This continues Chapter 1’s emphasis that the same number can tell different stories in different contexts.
Students should not interpret numbers against personal intuition when an institutional standard or process definition exists.
This concept prepares students for later geospatial, forecasting, streaming, and multimodal applications where external data may be analytically valuable.

text: Stakeholder Tension and Competing Objectives
Stakeholders may value different outcomes.
Marketing may prioritize acquisition; finance may prioritize margin; operations may prioritize workload stability; customers may prioritize affordability.
Analytics should expose trade-offs rather than pretending there is always one universally “best” answer.
Stakeholder Questions for Problem Framing:
Who owns the need?
Who has authority to decide?
Who is affected by the current condition?
Who provides or controls the data?
Who will use the output?
Who can explain domain meaning?
Who may bear the cost of errors?
Who defines what success means?
notes: This is one reason KPIs must be linked to objectives and stakeholders, not selected merely because they are easy to calculate.
The answer to these questions determines requirements, evaluation criteria, communication style, and responsible-use considerations.

A stakeholder map is a structured representation of stakeholder roles, interests, influence, needs, and expected participation.
Common dimensions include influence/power, interest, impact, data ownership, decision authority, and implementation responsibility.
The map is a thinking tool; it should be adapted to the project rather than used mechanically.

IIBA defines a stakeholder requirement as a description of the needs of a particular stakeholder or stakeholder class that must be met to achieve business requirements.
Stakeholder requirements bridge broad organizational goals and concrete solution expectations.
Examples: finance needs margin by channel; management needs a one-page decision brief; operations needs weekly alerts.

text: Requirement

IIBA describes a requirement broadly as a usable representation of a need. Requirements state conditions, capabilities, information, or qualities that must be satisfied. In analytics, requirements can concern business outcomes, stakeholder needs, data, outputs, quality, governance, timing, or technical operation.
Requirement Type
Definition
NEXUS Fulfillment Example
Business Requirement
States the organizational goal, objective, or desired outcome explaining why the initiative exists.
“Improve fulfillment reliability while controlling operating cost.”
Stakeholder Requirement
States what a particular stakeholder needs in order to perform a role, make a decision, or receive value from the initiative.
“Dispatch supervisors need early identification of orders likely to miss the SLA.”
Data Requirement
Specifies the information needed to answer analytics questions and evaluate success, including relevant entities, attributes, time coverage, grain, quality, and source.
Order timestamps, packing time, dispatch time, courier assignment, promised delivery date, actual delivery time, destination zone, and complaint records.
Output Requirement
Defines the analytical deliverable or result that must be produced and the form in which it should support stakeholder use.
An SLA-risk dashboard with prioritized late-risk orders, courier/zone breakdowns, and an exportable exception list.
Objectives, Metrics, KPIs, and Success
Analytics Question
An analytics question is a clearly formulated question that can be investigated using evidence and analysis to improve understanding or support a decision.
A good analytics question specifies the phenomenon, relevant population or unit, comparison or outcome, and decision relevance where possible.
It should be answerable with evidence rather than opinion alone.
Characteristics of a Good Analytics Question
Relevant to the problem and decision.
Specific enough to investigate.
Measurable or observable with appropriate evidence.

text: Analytics
What It Asks
Typical Analytical Operations
Example
Key Caution
Descriptive
What happened, what is happening, or how is performance distributed?
Aggregation, summarization, counts, rates, distributions, trends, observed segmentation
“How did revenue, gross profit, and order volume change from June to July?”
Establish the factual pattern first before attempting explanation.
Diagnostic
Why might an observed pattern have occurred?
Comparisons, relationships, decomposition, cohort analysis, contextual analysis, contributing-factor analysis
“Which channels, customer types, categories, and discount patterns coincide with weaker July profitability?”
Usually supports association, not automatic causal proof; use wording such as associated with, coincides with, or is consistent with unless causality is supported.
Predictive
What unknown, future, or unobserved outcome is likely?
Classification, regression, forecasting, risk scoring, probability estimation
“Which current customers are at elevated risk of not purchasing again within 60 days?”
Specify the target, unit of prediction, prediction/forecast horizon, and intended decision use. Prediction without a decision may have little operational value.
Prescriptive
What should be done given objectives, alternatives, and constraints?
Optimization, simulation, scenario analysis, decision rules, what-if analysis
“Which discount policy best balances gross-profit improvement and acceptable order-volume loss?”
Prediction and prescription are different: knowing what may happen does not by itself determine the best action.
Goal vs. Objective
Goal
A goal is a broad desired direction or state.
Goals provide strategic orientation but may be too broad for direct measurement.
Example: “Achieve sustainable retail growth.”
Objective
IIBA defines a business objective as an objective, measurable result indicating that a business goal has been achieved.
An analytics objective expresses the specific improvement or understanding the project seeks to achieve.
Examples: improve gross margin; reduce churn; increase service coverage; shorten response time.
notes: Goals should be translated into objectives and indicators before analytics can evaluate progress.
Objectives should describe desired change, not simply activities such as “build a dashboard.”

text: Activity vs. Output vs. Outcome vs. Impact
Level
Expanded Meaning
Key Question
Retail Analytics Example
Activity
The work, task, or process performed by the project team using available resources. Activities describe what the team does, not what changes because of the work.
What did we do?
Clean and integrate June–July transaction data, calculate profitability measures, and build the KNIME workflow.
Output
The immediate product, deliverable, or analytical result produced directly by the activity. Outputs are generally within the project team's direct control.
What did we produce?
Channel profitability analysis, KPI tables, margin visualizations, and a decision-support report identifying where profitability weakened.
Outcome

A change in behavior, decision, process, capability, or performance that occurs because stakeholders use the output. Outcomes depend not only on producing analytics, but also on whether stakeholders understand, accept, and act on it.
What changed because the output was used?
Management revises discount rules for low-margin channels and changes promotional priorities based on the analysis.
Impact
The broader and more meaningful value or long-term effect resulting from the outcomes. Impact reflects why the initiative ultimately mattered to the organization or beneficiaries.
Why did the change matter?
Gross margin improves while order growth remains sustainable, producing healthier and more profitable retail growth over time.

text: Leading Indicator vs. Lagging Indicator
Leading Indicator
A leading indicator provides an earlier signal about conditions that may influence future outcomes.
It is useful for proactive management but may have weaker direct connection to final outcomes.
Examples: discount intensity, repeat engagement, unresolved tickets, inventory stockout rate.
Lagging Indicator
A lagging indicator measures an outcome after it has occurred.
Examples: monthly gross profit, churn rate, graduation rate, total program completion, annual donations.
Lagging indicators are important for accountability but may arrive too late for intervention.
notes: Leading indicators should be empirically and conceptually linked to outcomes; merely occurring earlier in time does not make a measure useful.
A balanced analytics design often combines leading and lagging indicators.

text: Target
A target is a desired value or level for a metric or KPI within a specified period.
Targets may come from strategy, policy, benchmarks, budgets, service-level agreements, or negotiated stakeholder expectations.
Targets should not be invented simply to make a dashboard look complete.

text: KPI Tree

A KPI tree (Key Performance Indicator tree) is a structured diagram that breaks down a main business objective into smaller, measurable components. These components branch out from high-level strategic goals to specific operational metrics that contribute to achieving those goals.

Think of it like a family tree for your business performance. At the top is your ultimate goal, such as “Increase company profitability.” From there, branches represent contributing factors like “Revenue Growth” and “Cost Optimization.” Each of these branches divides further into measurable KPIs such as “Customer Acquisition Rate” or “Operational Efficiency.”

text: The Structure of a KPI Tree
Level
Component
Meaning
Example
Key Question
Level 1
Strategic Objective
The highest-level organizational goal the KPI tree is intended to support. It is often linked to the organization’s strategy, mission, or desired business outcome.
Increase profitability; improve customer satisfaction; grow market share; enhance operational efficiency
What are we ultimately trying to achieve?
Level 2
Key Drivers
Broad performance areas that contribute to achieving the strategic objective. These explain the major dimensions through which performance can improve or deteriorate.
For profitability: Revenue Growth and Cost Reduction
What major factors drive this objective?
Level 3
Sub-Drivers / Supporting Metrics
More specific components that break each key driver into measurable areas of performance and help explain how the driver behaves.
Under Revenue Growth: New Customer Acquisition, Customer Retention, Average Order Value
What components explain or influence each key driver?
Level 4
Operational KPIs / Measures
Specific, actionable measures that can be tracked regularly at the operational level and used to monitor activities or conditions contributing to higher-level performance.
Conversion Rate, Customer Churn Rate, Delivery Time, Marketing Cost per Lead
What can we regularly measure and act upon?
How to build your KPI Tree
Step
What to Do
Example
1. Define the Strategic Objective
Start with the ultimate organizational outcome to be achieved. The objective should be clear, measurable, realistic, and aligned with business goals.
Increase profit margin by 10%; achieve 95% customer satisfaction; improve SLA compliance to 95%.
2. Identify Key Performance Drivers
Determine the broad factors or performance areas that materially influence the strategic objective.
Revenue Growth, Cost Reduction, Customer Experience, Fulfillment Reliability.
3. Break Drivers into Measurable Indicators
Decompose each driver into more specific sub-drivers, KPIs, and supporting operational measures that can be monitored.
Customer Satisfaction → Response Time, Complaint Rate, NPS; Fulfillment Reliability → Dispatch Waiting Time, On-Time Courier Pickup %.
4. Validate the Relationships
Check whether each measure has a logical, operational, mathematical, or evidence-supported relationship with the higher-level driver or objective. Remove weak or arbitrary links.
If Packing Time has little relationship with SLA performance, reconsider whether it belongs on the main tree.
5. Assign Ownership
Designate a person, team, or organizational unit responsible for monitoring and acting on each important KPI.
Dispatch Manager owns On-Time Courier Pickup %; Customer Service owns Complaint Resolution Time.
6. Visualize the KPI Tree
Organize the objective, drivers, KPIs, and supporting measures into a clear hierarchical diagram that makes relationships easy to interpret.
Strategic Objective → Driver → Sub-Driver → KPI / Operational Measure.
7. Review and Refine
Reassess the KPI tree as strategies, processes, stakeholder needs, and operating conditions change. Remove irrelevant measures and add new ones when justified.
Revisit the tree after a new courier model, pricing policy, or fulfillment process is introduced.

Scope
IIBA defines scope as the boundaries of control, change, a solution, or a need.
In analytics, scope specifies what population, process, time period, geography, variables, decisions, and outputs are included or excluded.
Clear scope prevents project drift and overclaiming.
Type
Meaning
NEXUS Fulfillment Example
Why It Matters
In Scope
Elements, processes, populations, variables, time periods, and questions that the analytics project intentionally includes and is expected to investigate.
Order preparation, packing, dispatch, courier assignment, destination zone, promised vs. actual delivery time, SLA compliance, and customer complaints for the selected analysis period.
Defines what the project is responsible for analyzing and what its findings may legitimately address.
Out of Scope
Elements that are explicitly excluded from the current analysis or iteration, even if they may be relevant to the broader organizational situation.
Supplier performance, product quality, payment disputes, merchant pricing strategy, employee compensation, and long-term courier-contract negotiations.
Prevents scope creep and avoids making claims that the available evidence or project mandate cannot support.

text: Defining the Analytical Boundaries
Concept
Meaning
Example
In Scope
Elements intentionally covered by the current analysis and for which the project is expected to produce evidence.
June–July transactions, customers, products, channels, discounts, revenue, and gross profit
Out of Scope
Elements explicitly excluded from the current iteration. They may still matter, but the project will not claim to answer them.
Competitor pricing, customer motivation, supplier negotiations
Analytical Grain
The unit represented by one row or observation in the analysis.
Transaction line, order, customer, customer-month
Granularity
The level of detail at which data or results are represented.
Daily vs. monthly; customer vs. segment
Time Horizon
The period covered by the analysis, prediction, or decision.
June–July; next 30 days; next quarter
Scope determines what we study; grain determines what one observation represents; granularity determines how detailed the view is; time horizon determines when the analysis applies.
notes: Important: Out of scope does not mean unimportant—it means the current evidence will not be used to make claims about it.

text: Assumptions, Constraints, and Dependencies
Concept
Meaning
Example
Assumption
A condition believed to be true for planning or analysis but not yet fully confirmed.
June and July are sufficiently comparable; cost fields are accurate
Constraint
A factor the team must work within that restricts possible solutions or choices.
Budget, deadline, privacy rules, staff capacity, system capability
Dependency
Something the project relies upon for progress, validity, or delivery.
Analysis depends on Finance providing cost data
Key distinction
Assumption → What are we treating as true?
Constraint → What limits what we can do?
Dependency → What must be available or happen for us to proceed?
Dependencies may become risks when their availability or completion is uncertain.
notes: Important: Out of scope does not mean unimportant—it means the current evidence will not be used to make claims about it.

text: Risk and Limitation
Concept
Meaning
Analytics Example
Risk
The effect of uncertainty on objectives; something uncertain that may affect the project, analysis, implementation, or organizational outcome.
Missing data may bias findings; model drift may reduce later performance
Limitation
A known boundary affecting what the analysis can validly conclude, estimate, or generalize.
No customer survey means motivation cannot be directly inferred
Analytics risks may include:
data risk;
model risk;
privacy/governance risk;
implementation risk;
interpretation risk;
stakeholder/adoption risk.
Important distinction:
Risk concerns what may happen; limitation concerns what we already know the analysis cannot fully do or claim.
notes: A limitation is not an apology—it is part of responsible analytics.

text: Association, Causation, and Confounding
Concept
Meaning
Retail Example
Association
Two variables or patterns are statistically or descriptively related.
Higher discounts coincide with lower gross margin
Causation
Changing one factor would change an outcome, given appropriate causal assumptions and design.
Reducing discount intensity itself leads to improved margin
Confounding
A third factor influences both the suspected cause and the outcome, distorting their apparent relationship.
Product category affects both discount level and gross margin
Why this matters
An association may arise because of:
causation;
reverse causation;
common causes;
selection effects;
measurement artifacts;
coincidence.
Therefore:
“Associated with” is not equivalent to “caused by.”
notes: “Associated with” is not equivalent to “caused by.”
Students do not need advanced causal inference yet—but they must avoid causal wording that the study design cannot support.

Concept
Meaning
Example
Trade-Off
Improving one objective may worsen another.
Higher profit vs. lower sales volume
Feasibility
Whether the proposed action can realistically be implemented under technical, financial, operational, legal, and human constraints.
A real-time prediction service may be too costly for the current infrastructure
Expected Value
The anticipated usefulness or benefit of improved information or decisions relative to costs, risks, and constraints.
Better discount decisions may protect profitable growth
Value may be:

Risk-reducing — preventing losses or failures
The technically strongest solution is not necessarily the most valuable or feasible solution.

text: What Is an Analytics Project Charter?

PMI describes a project charter as a high-level document that establishes the project's objectives, scope, major deliverables, assumptions, constraints, risks, responsibilities, and criteria for success.
An Analytics Project Charter is a concise alignment document that connects:
Problem → Stakeholders → Decision → Analytics Questions → Evidence → Success Criteria → Scope → Expected Value
before substantial technical work begins.
Why it matters? Because a charter:
creates shared understanding;
prevents scope drift;
prevents tool-driven detours;
makes assumptions and risks explicit;
defines what success means;
provides a reference for later analytical decisions.
notes: The charter answers “Why are we doing this?” before the workflow answers “How are we doing it?”

text: So, What Exactly Is the NEXUS Problem?

Is NEXUS facing a warehouse problem, delivery-capacity problem, service-communication problem, customer-expectation problem, or some combination?
